name: 4-channel SSR module (G3MB-202P, low level trigger)
description: Four Omron G3MB-202P solid state relays (phototriac, zero-cross, built-in snubber) on one board, each with a 2 A resistive fuse and status LED: GPIOs switch four separate AC mains loads of 0.1-2 A at 75-264 VAC with no moving contacts. AC loads only: a triac does not turn off on DC. Inputs are low level trigger (CH low = SSR on). Module supply 5 VDC (SSR input range 4-6 VDC). Sold as: 5V 4 Channel SSR G3MB-202P Solid State Relay Module 240V 2A Output with Resistive Fuse, low level trigger (input header DC+, DC-, CH1, CH2, CH3, CH4 on one edge; a 2-way output screw terminal per channel on the opposite edge).
eli5: Four silent electronic switches for mains-powered things like lamps or heaters: when your board pulls CH1, CH2, CH3 or CH4 low, that lamp gets power.

pins.name: DC+
pins.description: Module supply, 5 V (SSR input rated 4-6 VDC, about 11-12.5 mA per SSR that is on plus its LED); use the board's 5V/VIN/VBUS pin, not 3V3

pins.name: CH1
pins.description: SSR 1 control input, LOW level trigger: 0-0.5 V = SSR 1 on, 3.3-5 V = off (0.5-3.3 V undefined). The GPIO sinks the SSR input and LED current (a few mA) while on.

pins.name: CH2
pins.description: SSR 2 control input, LOW level trigger: 0-0.5 V = SSR 2 on, 3.3-5 V = off (0.5-3.3 V undefined). The GPIO sinks the SSR input and LED current (a few mA) while on.

pins.description: SSR 3 control input, LOW level trigger: 0-0.5 V = SSR 3 on, 3.3-5 V = off (0.5-3.3 V undefined). The GPIO sinks the SSR input and LED current (a few mA) while on.

supplierQuery: 4 channel 5V SSR G3MB-202P solid state relay module low level trigger resistive fuse
buildNotes: Low level trigger: CH low = SSR on, CH high = off. Create the pins with value=1 so the loads do not switch on while the board boots; a GPIO that idles low turns its channel on.

Vendor thresholds: 0-0.5 V = on, 3.3-5 V = off (some listings quote 0-2.5 V as the trigger range). A 3.3 V GPIO high sits right at the edge of 'off': it usually switches off, but if a load stays on or glows, drive each CH through an NPN transistor (GPIO -> 1 kOhm -> base, emitter to GND, collector to CH; logic then inverts: GPIO high = on) or a 5 V logic buffer. Do not pull CH up to 5 V with a 3.3 V pin connected.

AC loads only (75-264 VAC, 0.1-2 A per channel). The triac never turns off on a DC load, and loads under 0.1 A (small LED bulbs) can glow or fail to switch off because of the snubber's leakage current (up to 1.5 mA at 200 VAC).
Zero-cross switching: each output changes at the next mains zero crossing (up to 1/2 cycle + 1 ms). It cannot dim (no phase control) and is too slow for PWM.

Mains wiring on the output screw terminals is dangerous: put each SSR in series with the live wire of its load, keep the board in a closed insulated box, and never touch it while plugged in. Leave mains to an adult/qualified person.

The input header (DC+, DC-, CH1-CH4) is on the opposite edge from the mains terminals, so wire it with jumper leads; it does not sit on a breadboard. Power DC+ from 5 V and share DC- with the microcontroller's GND.

Both low- and high-level-trigger versions of this board are sold and look alike: check the listing/silkscreen says low level trigger. Derate the 2 A rating when hot: Omron says halve the load current when SSRs are mounted close together or ventilation is poor.

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

# Low level trigger: CH low = SSR on, CH high = off.
# Create every pin HIGH (value=1) so no load switches on at boot.
ssr = [Pin(n, Pin.OUT, value=1) for n in ({CH1}, {CH2}, {CH3}, {CH4})]
while True:
    ssr[0].value(0)
    ssr[2].value(0)
    ssr[1].value(1)
    ssr[3].value(1)
    print('SSR 1+3 ON, 2+4 OFF')
    time.sleep(2)
    ssr[0].value(1)
    ssr[2].value(1)
    ssr[1].value(0)
    ssr[3].value(0)
    print('SSR 1+3 OFF, 2+4 ON')
    time.sleep(2)
